Author: S. Li
Title: Uncovering neuroinflammation-related modules and potential repurposing drugs for Alzheimer's disease through multi-omics data integrative analysis
Functional facet: Alzheimer's disease and Abeta accumulation and Neuroinflammation
Notes: WGCNA identified 16 co-expression modules in AD vs. control PFC microarray data (GSE44770); the green module (AIM) showed the highest correlation with Abeta accumulation and neuroinflammation. Immune-related genes were extracted by intersecting the full AIM module with ImmunPort immune gene lists, yielding this 44-gene set.

Author: H. Mathys
Title: Single-cell atlas reveals correlates of high cognitive function, dementia, and resilience to Alzheimer's disease pathology
Location in the paper: Custom re-analysis by J. Willett (Prokopenko/Tanzi Lab, MGH) of the Mathys 2023 dataset; not in the paper's supplementary tables. Source object: single_cell_outcome_cogimpairment_orpathology_fdr_5e-2.rds; contrast 4v3 (group 4 = pathology + cognitive impairment vs group 3 = pathology + preserved cognition); FDR<0.05; no logFC cutoff.
Notes: Genes with higher expression in cognitively resilient individuals (group 3: AD-like pathology + preserved cognition) relative to AD individuals (group 4: pathology + cognitive impairment) in astrocytes of the dorsolateral PFC. Directionality follows the first-term (Resilience) convention: 'up' = up in resilience (AvgLog2FC<0 in the 4v3 contrast). N=1194 genes at FDR<0.05, no logFC threshold. Categorical proxy for the paper's continuous cognitive-resilience score analysis.

Author: H. Mathys
Title: Single-cell atlas reveals correlates of high cognitive function, dementia, and resilience to Alzheimer's disease pathology
Location in the paper: Custom re-analysis by J. Willett (Prokopenko/Tanzi Lab, MGH) of the Mathys 2023 dataset; not in the paper's supplementary tables. Source object: single_cell_outcome_cogimpairment_orpathology_fdr_5e-2.rds; contrast 4v3 (group 4 = pathology + cognitive impairment vs group 3 = pathology + preserved cognition); FDR<0.05; no logFC cutoff.
Notes: Genes with lower expression in cognitively resilient individuals (group 3: AD-like pathology + preserved cognition) relative to AD individuals (group 4: pathology + cognitive impairment) in astrocytes of the dorsolateral PFC. Directionality follows the first-term (Resilience) convention: 'down' = down in resilience (AvgLog2FC>0 in the 4v3 contrast). N=1117 genes at FDR<0.05, no logFC threshold. Categorical proxy for the paper's continuous cognitive-resilience score analysis.

Author: J.B. Williams
Title: Transcriptomic analysis of human brains with Alzheimer's disease reveals the altered expression of synaptic genes linked to cognitive deficits
Notes: Downregulated synaptic genes in AD vs. CTR (129 AD, 101 CTR; postmortem PFC, GSE44770); 239 SynGO-annotated synaptic genes filtered from the full DEG list (adj. p < 0.05, |FC| > 1.1 via Limma); represents the synaptic-specific subset of the AD transcriptomic signature.

Author: K. Breuer
Title: InnateDB: systems biology of innate immunity and beyond
Notes: This study used microarrays to analyse changes in blood leukocyte gene expression patterns in human subjects receiving an inflammatory stimulus (bacterial endotoxin). Here they evaluate the genome-wide response to systemic inflammation in the context of a fully predictable recovery. Gene expression in whole blood leukocytes was determined immediately before and at 2, 4, 6, 9 and 24 h after the intravenous administration of bacterial endotoxin to four healthy human subjects. Four additional subjects were studied under identical conditions but without endotoxin administration.

Author: H. Mathys
Title: Single-cell atlas reveals correlates of high cognitive function, dementia, and resilience to Alzheimer's disease pathology
Location in the paper: Custom re-analysis by J. Willett (Prokopenko/Tanzi Lab, MGH) of the Mathys 2023 dataset; not in the paper's supplementary tables. Source object: single_cell_outcome_cogimpairment_orpathology_fdr_5e-2.rds; contrast 4v3 (group 4 = pathology + cognitive impairment vs group 3 = pathology + preserved cognition); FDR<0.05; no logFC cutoff.
Notes: Genes with lower expression in cognitively resilient individuals (group 3: AD-like pathology + preserved cognition) relative to AD individuals (group 4: pathology + cognitive impairment) in cortical interneurons of the dorsolateral PFC. Directionality follows the first-term (Resilience) convention: 'down' = down in resilience (AvgLog2FC>0 in the 4v3 contrast). N=1037 genes at FDR<0.05, no logFC threshold. Categorical proxy for the paper's continuous cognitive-resilience score analysis.

Author: M. Olah
Title: Single cell RNA sequencing of human microglia uncovers a subset associated with Alzheimer’s disease
Notes: Marker genes upregulated in Cluster 1 (Homeostatic microglia) relative to all other microglial clusters, by scRNA-seq of live-purified microglia from human cerebral cortex (17 donors: 14 dorsolateral prefrontal cortex autopsy from the Rush Memory and Aging Project + 3 temporal cortex surgical resection from Brigham and Women's Hospital for epilepsy surgery). Clusters defined by iterative PCA-Louvain clustering with random-forest robustness validation (>=75% prediction accuracy). Filter: edgeR on un-normalized counts; gene must be significantly upregulated in target cluster vs every other cluster (all pairwise comparisons significant, no downregulation permitted). n=57 genes. Homeostatic identity shared with Cluster 2 (Notes on GL0000233).

Author: G. L. Stein-O’Brien
Title: Transcriptional Signatures of Hippocampal Tau Pathology in Primary Age-Related Tauopathy and Alzheimer’s Disease
Location in the paper: Supplementary Table 2 (mmc2.xlsx), sheet 'AD FC'; DEG list in Tau-Positive versus Tau-Negative Neurons in AD.
Notes: Downregulated genes in tau-pathology-bearing (AT8-positive, containing intraneuronal tau accumulation) cornu ammonis 1 pyramidal neurons compared to adjacent tau-pathology-free (AT8-negative) cornu ammonis 1 pyramidal neurons (12 genes). Contrast type: this is a WITHIN-Alzheimer's-disease contrast — tau-positive and tau-negative neurons are BOTH profiled from the same Alzheimer's disease donors (n=6 Alzheimer's disease cases). It is NOT a disease-versus-control comparison; although the parent paper also profiled control tissue and primary age-related tauopathy tissue separately, this list is derived exclusively from within-donor tau-positive vs tau-negative comparisons in the Alzheimer's disease cohort. Tissue: hippocampus. Method: GeoMx digital spatial transcriptomics. Filter: absolute log2 fold change greater than 0.2 AND false discovery rate less than 0.05 (mixed-effects linear model, tau-positive minus tau-negative contrast).

Author: L. E. de Vries
Title: Gene-expression profiling of individuals resilient to Alzheimer's disease reveals higher expression of genes related to metallothionein and mitochondrial processes and no changes in the unfolded protein response

Notes: Genes down-regulated in cognitively resilient individuals relative to symptomatic AD (bulk RNA-seq of superior frontal gyrus, DESeq2, adjusted p ≤ 0.10, log2FoldChange < 0). Notes: Top 200 genes for GEP Exc1 in excitatory neurons, pooled across all 48 subjects and all 6 brain regions (EC, HC, TH, AG, MT, PFC). Gene expression programs (GEPs) were identified using consensus non-negative matrix factorisation (cNMF; Kotliar et al. eLife 2019). cNMF decomposes the single-cell gene expression matrix into k latent programs by iteratively running NMF with random initialisations and retaining only the most reproducible solutions (consensus step). The optimal k was selected based on stability and reconstruction error across initialisations. Each GEP represents a co-expression module: a set of genes that vary together across cells: and each cell receives a continuous usage score for every program simultaneously. Programs are not discrete clusters; they capture shared transcriptional states that may span multiple cell subtypes. Genes are ranked by their NMF loading weight; the top 200 are reported here.

Gene expression programs (GEPs) were identified using consensus non-negative matrix factorisation (cNMF; Kotliar et al. eLife 2019). cNMF decomposes the single-cell gene expression matrix into k latent programs by iteratively running NMF with random initialisations and retaining only the most reproducible solutions (consensus step). The optimal k was selected based on stability and reconstruction error across initialisations. Each GEP represents a co-expression module: a set of genes that vary together across cells: and each cell receives a continuous usage score for every program simultaneously. Programs are not discrete clusters; they capture shared transcriptional states that may span multiple cell subtypes. Genes are ranked by their NMF loading weight; the top 200 are reported here.

Author: T. Kamath
Title: Single-cell genomic profiling of human dopamine neurons identifies a population that selectively degenerates in Parkinson's disease
Notes: Marker genes for the SOX6_AGTR1 dopaminergic neuron subtype of the human substantia nigra pars compacta, identified by single-nucleus RNA sequencing of postmortem midbrain tissue from 8 neurotypical donors and 10 individuals with Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia (Kamath et al. 2022). Genes were selected as enriched in the SOX6_AGTR1 subtype relative to all other dopaminergic neuron subtypes using the MAST mixed-effects hurdle model with a false discovery rate threshold of less than 0.05 (Benjamini-Hochberg correction) and a positive discrete-component coefficient (MAST-D > 0), indicating higher expression prevalence in SOX6_AGTR1 cells; 3500 genes retained.

Author: A. Lu
Title: Human microglial transitions at the Abeta–tau inflection point associate with divergent pathways to dementia and resilience
Location in the paper: Supplementary Table 3 (Early and late PIGs); Fig. 3c
Notes: Amyloid-induced microglial "plaque-induced gene" program (Early PIGs): 81 genes upregulated in microglia in response to Aβ pathology in the absence of tau. Dominated by complement (C1QA, C1QB, C1QC, C3) and TREM2–TYROBP signalling. In the paper this program is predominantly expressed by the Mic_5 microglial state. How it was defined: leading-edge subset (GSEA) of the OCT-GreenYellow WGCNA module (172 microglia-enriched, AD-GWAS-enriched genes) along the A axis (A+T− vs A−T− spots; module GSEA NES=3.32, FDR≈0). Axes built from 16,629 Visium spots in cortical layers 3–5 of 16 octogenarian donors; pathology quantified per spot as percent overlap with 4G8 (Aβ) and AT8 (pTau) immunofluorescence on the same tissue section. No per-gene fold-change threshold — leading-edge membership only.

Author: E. Gerrits
Title: Distinct amyloid-β and tau-associated microglia profiles in Alzheimer’s disease
Location in the paper: Supplementary Table 7 (401_2021_2263_MOESM2_ESM.xlsx); block 'AD1 vs homeostasis'; up direction (adjusted p-value < 0.05 AND |log2 fold change| > 0.15).
Notes: Genes upregulated in AD1 compared to homeostatic microglia in human cortical brain tissue (417 genes). AD1 microglia (subclusters 7,9,10) This population shares transcriptional features with the phagocytic, activated microglia profile reported in amyloid mouse models (markers include ITGAX, LPL, GPNMB, MYO1E, and SPP1), is enriched for gene ontology terms including cell migration, phagocytosis, and lipid localisation, and its relative abundance strongly and positively correlates with tissue amyloid-beta load in samples containing amyloid-beta pathology only. Homeostatic microglia (subclusters 0, 1, and 5) are enriched for homeostasis marker genes such as P2RY12 and CX3CR1. Contrast: pooled AD1 subclusters versus pooled homeostatic subclusters, within the same single-nucleus RNA sequencing dataset comprising ten Alzheimer's disease donors and eight non-demented control donors. Tissue: occipital cortex and occipitotemporal cortex (pooled). Method: single-nucleus RNA sequencing; differential gene expression by logistic regression with donor identity as a latent variable. Filter: adjusted p-value less than 0.05 AND absolute log fold-change greater than 0.15 (the paper's own significance criterion for subcluster-enriched genes).

Author: C. Sanchez
Title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen identifies protein pathways modulating tau protein levels in neurons
Notes: Genes whose CRISPR knockout increased total endogenous tau protein levels in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells (n=62). Design: genome-wide pooled CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen (TKOv3-style whole-genome gRNA library), FACS-sorted into low/high total-tau populations (SP70 antibody) at 21- and 30-day post-transduction timepoints. Primary-screen candidates required an RSA up score of < -3 at both timepoints (215 candidates total for this direction); this list is restricted to the subset independently confirmed as reproducible hits (RSA score <= -5) in at least 2 of 6 secondary custom mini-pool validation screens (62 of 215, 29%), the paper's own final validated gene set (Supplementary Data 6, sheet 'Up regulating'). Directionality note: 'up' here means the KNOCKOUT increased tau protein abundance - this is a functional-screen phenotype direction, NOT a disease-vs-control expression contrast, and should not be read as 'upregulated in disease'. Facet rationale (Tau degradation, not Tau clearance): the paper itself uses the word 'clearance' only once, hedged, for a single gene pair (TSC1/TSC2: 'could impact tau clearance' as one of two competing hypotheses, followed by a negative validation result) - it does not claim this gene set broadly represents tau clearance. This screen is a single-cell-type (SH-SY5Y monoculture) assay with no extracellular or intercellular compartment, so it cannot speak to the extracellular disposal mechanisms included in the Genedex 'Tau clearance' facet definition (microglial uptake, BBB efflux, etc.). 'Tau degradation' - intracellular breakdown via UPS/autophagy-lysosome only - is the better-scoped facet: it matches the paper's own reported pathway enrichment for this gene set (mTOR signalling and endolysosomal membrane proteins), while still being an inference from pathway identity rather than a directly demonstrated degradation-rate measurement (the screen measured steady-state tau protein level only, not autophagic flux or proteasome activity). Cell system: human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line (immortalized, not primary/patient tissue) - a commonly used in vitro neuronal model, not a genuine neuronal cellular facet from tissue.

Author: C. Sanchez
Title: Genome-wide CRISPR screen identifies protein pathways modulating tau protein levels in neurons
Notes: Genes whose CRISPR knockout decreased total endogenous tau protein levels in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells (n=93), including MAPT itself (the tau gene, included by the paper's own hit-calling pipeline and originally used by the authors as an internal positive control for screen sensitivity). Design: genome-wide pooled CRISPR-Cas9 knockout screen (TKOv3-style whole-genome gRNA library), FACS-sorted into low/high total-tau populations (SP70 antibody) at 21- and 30-day post-transduction timepoints. Primary-screen candidates required an RSA down score of < -3 at both timepoints (266 candidates total for this direction); this list is restricted to the subset independently confirmed as reproducible hits (RSA score <= -5) in at least 2 of 6 secondary custom mini-pool validation screens (93 of 266, 35%), the paper's own final validated gene set (Supplementary Data 6, sheet 'Down regulating'). Directionality note: 'down' here means the KNOCKOUT decreased tau protein abundance (i.e. these genes normally support tau expression, transcription, or stability) - this is a functional-screen phenotype direction, NOT a disease-vs-control expression contrast, and should not be read as 'downregulated in disease'. Facet rationale: this is NOT a clearance/degradation gene set (that would be the genes whose loss INCREASES tau, see GL0001576/'Tau clearance') - these genes are required for tau to be present in the first place. STRING pathway enrichment highlighted E3 ubiquitin ligases, chromatin-modifying enzymes (e.g. BRD2), and RNA-metabolism genes, consistent with roles in tau transcription/production or protein stability rather than its removal. No existing Genedex facet captured this, so a new facet 'Tau production' was added to Functional_facets.csv (defined: generation/maintenance of tau protein abundance via transcriptional, chromatin-mediated, and post-translational mechanisms, as distinct from removal via clearance pathways). Cell system: human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cell line (immortalized, not primary/patient tissue) - a commonly used in vitro neuronal model, not a genuine neuronal cellular facet from tissue.
